questions.prompt: A Node housekeeping timer calls unref(), and no other work keeps the event loop active. What can happen to the process?

choices.text: It must wait for that timer.
It cancels the timer and permanently prevents its callback from executing.
It can exit before the timer fires.
It creates a worker thread that keeps the process alive until timeout.

questions.explanation: unref changes whether the timer keeps the event loop running. It does not cancel it; a process with no other active work may exit before its callback.

sources.title: Timers | Node.js v26.11.1 Documentation
sources.claim: Node timer unref prevents that timer alone from keeping the event loop active; it does not cancel the timer or guarantee execution.

questions.prompt: A Node app resolves a hostname with dns.lookup and expects an /etc/hosts entry to apply. Which resolution path explains this expectation?

choices.text: Direct DNS-protocol resolution.
A process-local hostname cache that bypasses operating-system resolver configuration.
An authoritative DNS lookup that ignores local host mappings and operating-system resolver settings.
Operating-system name resolution.

questions.explanation: dns.lookup uses the operating system facilities, which can consult hosts configuration. dns.resolve uses DNS protocol queries and a different resolution path.

sources.title: DNS | Node.js v26.11.1 Documentation
sources.claim: dns.lookup uses operating-system resolution with libuv thread-pool work; dns.resolve queries DNS without using the same OS lookup path.

questions.prompt: A Node HTTP server configures distinct timeouts for slow clients. Which meanings are accurate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: keepAliveTimeout is the maximum duration of every active response body.
headersTimeout limits the time to receive complete request headers.
requestTimeout limits the time to receive the entire request.
keepAliveTimeout concerns an idle connection after a response finishes.
requestTimeout is a guaranteed deadline for all application handler work.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: its idle period applies after response completion. B is correct: it protects the header-receiving phase. C is correct: it concerns inbound request reception rather than handler completion. D is correct: it sets the wait for additional incoming data on a reusable connection. E is incorrect: it times receipt of the request, not completion of arbitrary application processing.

sources.title: HTTP | Node.js v26.11.1 Documentation
sources.claim: headersTimeout bounds receiving complete headers; requestTimeout bounds receiving the full request; keepAliveTimeout follows response completion before idle socket destruction.

questions.prompt: A Node service unrefs a timeout while other requests keep the process alive. Which statement about that timeout is correct?

choices.text: Its callback can still execute.
Its callback is immediately cancelled.
It becomes an interval that repeats until ref is called again.
It is forced to execute synchronously before unref returns to the caller.

questions.explanation: An unrefed timer remains scheduled but does not keep the process alive on its own. clearTimeout is the separate cancellation operation.

sources.title: Timers | Node.js v26.11.1 Documentation
sources.claim: Node timer unref prevents that timer alone from keeping the event loop active; it does not cancel the timer or guarantee execution.

questions.prompt: A Node app performs many dns.lookup calls alongside other libuv-pool operations. Which shared resource can become contended?

choices.text: The request-handler JavaScript thread.
The libuv worker pool.
The asynchronous DNS-query path used by dns.resolve, independent of the libuv thread pool.
A dedicated permanent thread created for each unique hostname lookup.

questions.explanation: dns.lookup uses getaddrinfo on the shared libuv worker pool. dns.resolve uses asynchronous DNS queries without that pool; dns.lookup does not create one dedicated thread per hostname.

sources.title: DNS | Node.js v26.11.1 Documentation
sources.claim: dns.lookup uses operating-system resolution with libuv thread-pool work; dns.resolve queries DNS without using the same OS lookup path.

questions.prompt: A Node API accepts a slow upload and then performs lengthy application processing. Which timeout distinctions should its operator retain? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Application processing may need its own explicit deadline.
requestTimeout starts only after the handler has sent its response.
A larger keepAliveTimeout automatically gives a handler more CPU execution time.
headersTimeout measures how long response headers take to reach the client.
A header timeout does not by itself cap the whole upload body duration.

questions.explanation: A is correct: requestTimeout limits receiving the request rather than arbitrary processing. B is incorrect: it governs incoming request reception. C is incorrect: that setting controls post-response idle connection handling. D is incorrect: it limits receiving the client's request headers. E is correct: headersTimeout applies to header reception; full-request timing has a separate control.

sources.title: HTTP | Node.js v26.11.1 Documentation
sources.claim: headersTimeout bounds receiving complete headers; requestTimeout bounds receiving the full request; keepAliveTimeout follows response completion before idle socket destruction.
